The trade-wind trough that was forecast to bring scattered showers
and a slight chance of thunderstorms today dissipated as the 
temperature inversion and drier air aloft continued. However, an 
approaching trade-wind trough currently around 150E is much more 
prominent, with robust troughing apparent in the most recent 
scatterometry passes, and a line of scattered showers seen on 
visible satellite. A ridge downstream will continue isolated light 
showers across the region through Saturday morning before the trough 
arrives Saturday afternoon, bringing scattered showers and strong 
localized gusts, similar to what was observed today at Saipan 
International Airport during a light rain shower. According to CIMSS 
MIMIC, Precipitable Water (PWAT) values associated with this trough 
are 2.0 to 2.5 inches, which highlights the uptick in moisture 
compared to the surrounding drier air. Model time heights indicate 
drier air aloft to continue, so thunderstorms are not a concern as of
now. This could change, though, depending on newer model runs. Once 
the trough exits Tinian and Saipan Sunday and Guam and Rota Sunday 
afternoon, isolated showers may return through the rest of the 
forecast period. Gentle to moderate trade winds could increase to 
moderate to fresh by the end of the weekend.

According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, Guam is abnormally dry (D0) 
and the CNMI remains neutral. Water conservation efforts are 
encouraged as the dry season approaches, which could worsen drought 
conditions within the next several weeks.

Marine/Surf...
Gentle to moderate trade winds will prevail through Saturday and 
increase to moderate Saturday night. Combined seas of 6 to 8 feet 
are comprised of an elevated north swell and a trade swell. Seas 
will briefly dip Saturday night but may increase back to 6 to 8 
feet around the middle of next week as the trade swell increases.

Hazardous surf of 7 to 10 feet and a high risk of rip currents will 
continue along north-facing reefs through Saturday afternoon. Surf is
elevated along east-facing reefs and may continue through the rest of
the forecast period as the trade swell persists. Models may have not 
initialized well enough based on higher combined seas observed by 
SOFAR buoy data and altimetry outside of our coastal waters, so the 
High Surf Advisory and High Rip Current Risk Statement was extended 
another 12 hours. The long-period north swell that originated from 
Typhoon Cempaka has most likely peaked today, but may take more time 
to subside.

Eastern Micronesia...
The Near-Equatorial Trough (NET) remains fragmented across 
Micronesia but will try to re-establish itself over the coming days. 
A fragmented portion remains over the RMI this afternoon and has 
produced scattered to numerous showers and isolated thunderstorms 
over the last day or so. This is expected to linger into Saturday as 
it shifts westward with shower chances dropping throughout the day as
the fragments weakens. As a result, have kept scattered shower 
chances and isolated thunderstorms in the forecast at Majuro through 
Saturday with drier weather expected to develop thereafter through 
early next week. Drier weather can be expected at Pohnpei and Kosrae 
through the weekend and into early next week. Model guidance is 
hinting at a return of wet weather across much of eastern Micronesia 
late next week, so stay tuned! Light to gentle winds are expected to 
persist through at least early next week across the region. Combined 
seas of 4 to 7 feet will generally prevail at all forecast sites 
through Saturday with seas dropping a foot or two starting late this 
weekend. Seas consist of a northeast, a north-northwest, and a small,
southeast swell.

Most of eastern Micronesia is experiencing abnormally dry (D0) 
drought conditions. Try to conserve water as we continue to
transition into the dry season. 

Western Micronesia...
The Near-Equatorial Trough (NET) is trying to re-establish itself
across western Micronesia. This is resulting in a band of moderate
convergence across Palau, but south of Yap and Chuuk. The band of
convergence is producing numerous showers and isolated thunderstorms
across Palau this afternoon. As we move through the weekend, this
convection looks to drift south a bit, ushering in a dry pattern to 
Palau beginning Sunday. This drier pattern now looks to be short- 
lived, as the NET looks to setup and bring increased convection to 
Chuuk Monday, followed by Palau and Yap Tuesday, lasting through at 
least midweek. These are not expected to be heavy rainfall producers,
and may do little to head off the anticipated drought concerns, but 
locally heavy rainfall is still a possibility. Either way, water 
conservation is still a priority.
